content.title: About
content.content: The king oyster mushroom (Pleurotus eryngii) is a large edible fungus with a thick, meaty cap and a delicate flavor reminiscent of seafood. It is cultivated in controlled environments and widely used in cuisines around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “king oyster” refers to its size and oyster‑like shape.
It grows on the stems and roots of herbaceous plants, especially on thistles.
It is one of the most protein‑dense mushrooms, containing more protein than many vegetables.
In Japan it is often called “king mushroom” and used in sushi and ramen.
The mushroom can absorb and break down certain pollutants, making it useful for bioremediation.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: King oyster mushrooms contain about 20 % protein by dry weight, making them an excellent plant‑based protein source.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of fresh mushrooms provide only about 35 kcal, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They are rich in thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and vitamin B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Contain ergothioneine and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes digestive health and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms, including king oyster.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Mushrooms contain purines, so people with gout should limit intake.

items.title: Consume fresh only
items.content: Old or improperly stored mushrooms can cause foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: King oyster mushrooms are versatile – they can be sautéed, roasted, stewed, or grilled. Slice them into strips for soups, stews, pasta, salads, or use as a meat substitute in vegetarian dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh mushrooms in a paper bag in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 5 days. For longer storage, blanch them 2–3 minutes and freeze.
